readings.title: Buckingham Palace
readings.challenge: Hear the same two lines come back in every stanza and listen for what changes.
readings.focus: A child’s questions and a nanny’s down-to-earth answers make a royal outing funny.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Buckingham Palace is the King’s home in London, where soldiers called guards take turns on duty: the “changing of the guard.” Alice was Christopher Robin’s nanny. A sentry-box is a little hut for a guard; a hundred pounds was a great deal of money.

excerpt.locator: “Buckingham Palace,” the whole poem; opens “They’re changing guard at Buckingham Palace— Christopher Robin went down with Alice.…”; closes “…think the King knows all about me?” “Sure to, dear, but it’s time for tea,” Says Alice.”.

questions.prompt: Which two lines begin every stanza? Say them together the next time through.
facilitatorNotes: “They’re changing guard at Buckingham Palace— / Christopher Robin went down with Alice.” The repeat sounds like marching, and like a child who keeps going back to the same exciting place.
evidence: They’re changing guard at Buckingham Palace—

questions.prompt: Does Christopher Robin ever see the King? What do they see instead?
facilitatorNotes: No. They see a guard in a sentry-box and a face at a window, but “it wasn’t the King’s.” The poem is about waiting for someone who never comes.
evidence: We looked for the King, but he never came.
A face looked out, but it wasn’t the King’s.

questions.prompt: What kind of things does Alice say about soldiers and kings? Are they grand or ordinary?
facilitatorNotes: Ordinary: socks, hard work, signing papers, not wanting the job. She brings the palace down to everyday size. Some children may hear her as wise, others as not very interested.
evidence: One of the sergeants looks after their socks
I wouldn’t be King for a hundred pounds

questions.prompt: In the last stanza Christopher Robin asks, “Do you think the King knows all about me?” Why do you think he asks? What does Alice’s answer show?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to matter to the important man he came to see. Alice says “Sure to, dear” kindly, then changes the subject to tea. Children may feel she is loving, or that she is not really listening; both fit.
evidence: Do you think the King knows all about me?
Sure to, dear, but it’s time for tea

readings.title: The Christening
readings.challenge: Listen for a made-up word that rhymes, and for the reason given for each name.
readings.focus: Choosing a name for a pet, and the reason the last name wins.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A christening is a ceremony where a baby is given a name. A dormouse is a small mouse-like animal with a long, furry tail. “’Cos” is a short way of saying “because.”

excerpt.locator: “The Christening,” the whole poem; opens “What shall I call My dear little dormouse? His eyes are small, But his tail is…”; closes “But I think I shall call him Jim, ’Cos I am so fond of him.”.

questions.prompt: The poem says the dormouse’s tail is “e-nor-mouse.” What real word is hiding in it, and why is it funny?
facilitatorNotes: Enormous, bent to rhyme with dormouse. Read it slowly in three parts as the poem writes it.
evidence: But his tail is e-nor-mouse.

questions.prompt: Name the three “Terrible” names. What reason goes with each?
facilitatorNotes: John and Jack because the tail goes on and on; James because the dormouse likes being called names. Notice how the lines for John go “on— / And on— / And on,” like the tail.
evidence: ’Cos his tail goes on—
’Cos he says he likes me calling him names

questions.prompt: Why does the child choose Jim in the end? How is that reason different from the others?
facilitatorNotes: “’Cos I am so fond of him.” The other names were about the tail or a game; the last is about love. Some children may prefer Terrible Jack; ask for their reason too.
evidence: But I think I shall call him Jim,
’Cos I am so fond of him.

readings.title: The Four Friends
readings.challenge: Keep four characters straight and notice which one the poem keeps coming back to.
readings.focus: Three big, noisy animals and one tiny snail who goes on a journey nobody notices.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A stall, a manger and a pen are places where animals are kept. A huffle is a little puff of breath. A rumpus is a loud, wild noise. A compass is a tool that shows which way is north.

excerpt.locator: “The Four Friends,” the whole poem; opens “Ernest was an elephant, a great big fellow, Leonard was a lion with a six-foot tail,…”; closes “…new tail, George was a goat, as I think I have mentioned, But James was only a snail.”.

questions.prompt: Who are the four friends, and what is each one?
facilitatorNotes: Ernest the elephant, Leonard the lion, George the goat, and James the snail. Ask which one is smallest.
evidence: Ernest was an elephant, a great big fellow,
And James was a very small snail.

questions.prompt: What happens when the snail makes his noise, “the huffle of a snail in danger”?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody hears him at all: the elephant and lion are far too loud. Ask the child to make a huffle.
evidence: And nobody heard him at all.

questions.prompt: James “reached the end of his brick.” Is that a big journey or a small one?
facilitatorNotes: For a snail it is a whole journey, with a compass. The poem takes his small trip as seriously as the elephant’s noise. Children may find it funny or brave; both fit.
evidence: James went a journey with the goat’s new compass
And he reached the end of his brick.

questions.prompt: The last line says “But James was only a snail.” What does “only” make you feel about James?
facilitatorNotes: It sounds like he matters less; yet the poem has followed him the whole way. Some children will feel sorry for him, others will say he was the hero.
evidence: But James was only a snail.

readings.title: Lines and Squares
readings.challenge: Tell what is real in the street from what the child imagines.
readings.focus: A pavement game becomes a world of hungry bears.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. London pavements are made of square stones with lines between them. A lair is a wild animal’s den. “Portant” is the child’s way of saying “important.”

excerpt.locator: “Lines and Squares,” the whole poem; opens “Whenever I walk in a London street, I’m ever so careful to watch my feet; And I keep in…”; closes “…And it’s ever so jolly to call out, “Bears, Just watch me walking in all the squares!””.

questions.prompt: What is the rule of the child’s game?
facilitatorNotes: Walk only in the squares and never step on a line. Try it on a floor with tiles or boards.
evidence: And I keep in the squares,

questions.prompt: What will happen to “the sillies who tread on the lines,” according to the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Bears waiting at the corners will eat them. The child invents the danger that makes the game exciting.
evidence: Who wait at the corners all ready to eat

questions.prompt: What do the bigger bears pretend? Why might they pretend that?
facilitatorNotes: That they only came to look for a friend, and that nobody cares how you walk; they want you to stop being careful. Some children may say the child is trying to trick himself into stepping on a line.
evidence: That they came round the corner to look for a friend;

questions.prompt: Is the child frightened of the bears, or enjoying them? Find a line that shows it.
facilitatorNotes: Mostly enjoying: “it’s ever so jolly to call out.” He is showing off to the bears. A child who hears a little fear too can point to “It’s ever so portant how you walk.”
evidence: And it’s ever so jolly to call out, “Bears,
It’s ever so portant how you walk.

readings.title: Brownie
readings.challenge: Notice the lines in brackets and who speaks them.
readings.focus: A child half-believes in a hidden creature, and the grown-up plays along.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A brownie is a small, helpful fairy creature from old stories that hides in houses. Nanny is the woman who looks after the child.

excerpt.locator: “Brownie,” the whole poem; opens “In a corner of the bedroom is a great big curtain, Someone lives behind it, but I don’t…”; closes “…They wriggle off at once because they’re all so tickly. (Nanny says they’re tickly too.)”.

questions.prompt: Where does the Brownie live?
facilitatorNotes: Behind the big curtain in a corner of the bedroom.
evidence: In a corner of the bedroom is a great big curtain,

questions.prompt: Why has the child never seen the Brownie properly?
facilitatorNotes: He goes “so quickly” and wriggles off, because Brownies are tickly. The poem gives a reason that also explains why there is nothing there.
evidence: Brownies never wait to say, “How do you do?”
They wriggle off at once because they’re all so tickly.

questions.prompt: Read the two lines in brackets again. What is Nanny doing?
facilitatorNotes: Agreeing with the child, or playing along: she “isn’t certain, too,” and says they’re tickly too. Some children may think Nanny really believes; others that she is being kind. Both can be argued.
evidence: (Nanny isn’t certain, too.)
(Nanny says they’re tickly too.)

readings.title: Independence
readings.challenge: Hear how a repeated phrase sounds like a child stamping a foot.
readings.focus: A small child is tired of being looked after.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Independence means being able to do things by yourself. The words in quotation marks are things grown-ups say.

excerpt.locator: “Independence,” the whole poem; opens “I never did, I never did, I never did like “Now take care, dear!” I never did, I never…”; closes “…did think much of “Not up there, dear!” It’s no good saying it. They don’t understand.”.

questions.prompt: What three things do grown-ups say that the child doesn’t like?
facilitatorNotes: “Now take care, dear!”, “Hold-my-hand,” and “Not up there, dear!” Let the child say them in a grown-up voice.
evidence: I never did, I never did, I never did like “Now take care, dear!”

questions.prompt: Why does the poem say “I never did” three times in every line?
facilitatorNotes: It sounds like a child stamping and insisting, getting crosser each time. Read one line quietly and one loudly; which fits better?
evidence: I never did, I never did, I never did want “Hold-my-hand”;

questions.prompt: Who are “They” in the last line? Are they right not to understand?
facilitatorNotes: The grown-ups. The child thinks they cannot see he is big enough. Some children will side with the child; others will say grown-ups keep you safe. The title gives the child’s side its name.
evidence: It’s no good saying it. They don’t understand.

readings.title: Nursery Chairs
readings.challenge: Keep track of four chairs and the four different games they become.
readings.focus: Pretend play turns ordinary chairs into places, and the last question turns back to the child himself.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A nursery was a child’s playroom. The Amazon is a great river in South America. A high chair is a tall chair for a little child at the table. “Round-the-World” is a sailor’s joke name for a place.
readings.contentNote: The first chair’s game imagines the Amazon’s Indigenous people, called “Indians” in the poem, as a band who obey the boy. This is a 1924 English child’s idea of adventure, not a true picture of anyone’s life.

excerpt.locator: “Nursery Chairs,” the whole poem with its four chair-poems; opens “One of the chairs is South America, One of the chairs is a ship at sea, One is a cage for…”; closes “…out in my ship to sea? Or get in my cage and be lions and tigers? Or—shall I be only Me?”.

questions.prompt: Name the four chairs and what each one becomes.
facilitatorNotes: South America, a lion’s cage, a ship at sea, and a chair where he pretends to be a baby of three. Point to a real chair and choose one.
evidence: One of the chairs is South America,
One is a cage for a great big lion,

questions.prompt: In the lion’s cage, the child frightens Nanny, then what does he do?
facilitatorNotes: He holds her tight and tells her not to be frightened. He is both the scary lion and the comforter. Ask why he might like being both.
evidence: Tell her not to be so frightened—

questions.prompt: In the first chair the boy only has to wave his hand, and the people “always understand.” Why might he like being in charge in this game?
facilitatorNotes: In pretend, he is in charge and everyone obeys. Some children may say it is unfair to the people in the game; that is worth talking about too, using the content note.
evidence: I simply wave my hand.
They always understand.

questions.prompt: The fourth chair is a real high chair, and he pretends to be “a baby of three.” Why is that funny? What is his last question?
facilitatorNotes: He is already a small child, so pretending to be a baby is a joke. The last question asks whether to play a game or “be only Me.” Children may say being Me is the best choice, or the dullest.
evidence: And that I am a baby of three.
Or—shall I be only Me?

readings.title: Market Square
readings.challenge: Follow the child’s money and the stalls he visits, and notice the surprise at the end.
readings.focus: A search through the market fails, and what he wanted turns up free on the common.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A penny, tuppence (two pence) and a sixpence were English coins. Lavender is a sweet-smelling flower; mackerel is a fish. A common is open grassy land anyone may walk on. The stall-keepers’ calls are in brackets.

excerpt.locator: “Market Square,” the whole poem; opens “I had a penny, A bright new penny, I took my penny To the market square. I wanted a…”; closes “…the people who sell sweet lavender, ’Cos they haven’t got a rabbit, not anywhere there!”.

questions.prompt: What does the child want, and how much money does he have each time?
facilitatorNotes: A rabbit. First a penny, then two pennies, then a sixpence, then nothing. Count them up together.
evidence: I wanted a rabbit,
I found a sixpence,

questions.prompt: What do the stalls sell instead? How does the child answer each seller?
facilitatorNotes: Lavender, mackerel and saucepans. Each time he asks for a rabbit with a reason: he doesn’t want lavender, doesn’t like mackerel, and they already have two saucepans.
evidence: “Have you got a rabbit, ’cos I don’t want lavender?”
“Could I have a rabbit, ’cos we’ve got two saucepans?”

questions.prompt: When he has “nuffin’,” where does he go, and what does he find?
facilitatorNotes: The common, where he sees little rabbits everywhere: they were never for sale, and they cost nothing.
evidence: I had nuffin’,
And I saw little rabbits

questions.prompt: Why is he “sorry for the people” at the end? Is he right?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks they are missing the best thing because they have no rabbit. It is a child’s idea of what matters; the sellers may not mind at all. Some children will say he has learned that the best things are free.
evidence: So I’m sorry for the people who sell fine saucepans,

readings.title: Disobedience
readings.challenge: Notice who is supposed to obey whom, and hear how the poem changes in the last stanza.
readings.focus: A three-year-old in charge of his mother turns the usual rules upside down.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Disobedience is not doing what you are told. A gown is a long dress. To be mislaid is to be lost, as if put down in the wrong place. Forty shillings was a reward in English money. To consult is to ask someone first. In the last stanza, “C/o” stands for “care of” and the stars hide letters of a word.

excerpt.locator: “Disobedience,” the whole poem; opens “James James Morrison Morrison Weatherby George Dupree Took great Care of his Mother,…”; closes “…said he: “You-must-never-go-down-to-the-end-of-the-town-if-you-don’t-go-down-with ME!””.

questions.prompt: Who gives the orders in this poem: the mother or the child?
facilitatorNotes: James James, though he is only three. Usually a parent says “never go off without me”; here the child says it. That is the joke of the title.
evidence:
Took great
Care of his Mother,
Though he was only three.
“You must never go down to the end of the town, if you don’t go down with me.”

questions.prompt: What does King John’s notice say about James’s mother?
facilitatorNotes: Lost, stolen or strayed; last seen wandering; forty shillings reward. It reads like a notice for a lost pet. Read it in a loud town-crier voice.
evidence: SEEMS TO HAVE BEEN MISLAID.

questions.prompt: The poem says “Now then, very softly.” How does the last stanza look and sound different?
facilitatorNotes: It is in short letters and stars, like a whispered secret or a code: J.J. for James James and M***** for Mother. Read it softly, as the poem asks, then the last line loudly.
evidence: (Now then, very softly)
C/o his M*****

questions.prompt: James’s mother “hasn’t been heard of since.” Is this sad, or funny, or both?
facilitatorNotes: The poem treats it as a joke, and everyone shrugs: “what can anyone do?” Some children will be worried about the mother; that feeling is fair too, and the silly whisper at the end tells us not to take it too hard.
evidence: Hasn’t been heard of since.
well, what can anyone do?

readings.title: The Three Foxes
readings.challenge: Listen for the extra “-es” endings that make the words silly.
readings.focus: Nonsense rhymes bend words to tell what three foxes did and didn’t do.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A copse is a small wood. A fair has games and prizes; at a coconut shy you throw balls to knock coconuts off stands. Mince-pies and plum-puddings are English sweet foods.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Foxes,” the whole poem; opens “Once upon a time there were three little foxes Who didn’t wear stockings, and they didn’t…”; closes “…they didn’t wear trousies, And they didn’t wear stockings and they didn’t wear sockses.”.

questions.prompt: What don’t the three little foxes wear? What do they have instead?
facilitatorNotes: No stockings, socks, coats or trousers, but handkerchiefs in cardboard boxes.
evidence: Who didn’t wear stockings, and they didn’t wear sockses,
And they kept their handkerchiefs in cardboard boxes.

questions.prompt: Find the silly words. What are the real words, and why did the poet change them?
facilitatorNotes: Sockses, trousies, mouses, wopses, mince-pieses, shieses. He bends words to rhyme with “foxes” and “houses,” and it sounds like a small child talking. Let the child invent one.
evidence: And they played “Touch last” with a family of mouses.
They went out hunting, and they caught three wopses.

questions.prompt: The poet says “That’s all that I know.” How does the last stanza wrap up the poem?
facilitatorNotes: It goes back to the first things we heard: handkerchiefs, houses, no coats, no socks. The ending sounds like the beginning turned round. Some children will notice the order is changed.
evidence: That’s all that I know of the three little foxes

readings.title: Politeness; Jonathan Jo
readings.challenge: In both poems, listen for asking and answering: what people ask for, and what they get back.
readings.focus: A polite child who is tired of being asked, and a cheerful man who gives whatever is asked.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. In “Politeness” the poet prints BUT SOMETIMES in capital letters and lets the last lines stand alone; pause before them. A wheelbarrow is a one-wheeled cart you push. A hoop and a top are old toys you roll and spin. An Aberdeen terrier is a small black dog.

excerpt.locator: “Politeness” and “Jonathan Jo,” two whole poems; opens “If people ask me, I always tell them: “Quite well, thank you, I’m very glad to say.” If…”; closes “…so funny: If you give him a smile, Only once in a while, Then he never expects any money!”.

questions.prompt: In “Politeness,” what does the child always answer? What surprise comes after BUT SOMETIMES?
facilitatorNotes: “Quite well, thank you,” every time; and then he admits he sometimes wishes people would not ask. Read the last lines slowly.
evidence: Quite well, thank you, I’m very glad to say.
That they wouldn’t.

questions.prompt: Why might a child wish people would stop asking how he is?
facilitatorNotes: He must give the same polite answer every time, even when he may not feel quite well. Children may have their own reasons; ask whether polite answers are always true ones.
evidence: BUT SOMETIMES

questions.prompt: What comes out of Jonathan Jo’s wheelbarrow? Name all you can remember.
facilitatorNotes: A bat, a ball, a hoop and a top, a watch that won’t stop, sweets, and an Aberdeen terrier.
evidence: And a wheelbarrow full of surprises;

questions.prompt: What does Jonathan Jo want in return? Why does that make him “so funny”?
facilitatorNotes: Only a smile once in a while, never any money. Funny here means unusual and surprising; some children will think it is his round “O” mouth. Both are in the poem.
evidence: But this is what makes him so funny:
Then he never expects any money!

readings.title: At the Zoo
readings.challenge: Listen for the line that ends every stanza, and the small words that change the last time.
readings.focus: A child lists all the amazing animals, but the one he loves is the one he can feed.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Some animal names are muddled on purpose: a “potamus” is a hippopotamus, a “nosserus” a rhinoceros, a “mingo” a flamingo, and a “wallaboo” is nearly a wallaby. A Superintendent is the person in charge. Buns are small sweet rolls.

excerpt.locator: “At the Zoo,” the whole poem; opens “There are lions and roaring tigers, and enormous camels and things, There are…”; closes “…hate saying, “How do you do?”— But I give buns to the elephant when I go down to the Zoo!”.

questions.prompt: Which animal names are real, and which are muddled? Can you fix the muddled ones?
facilitatorNotes: Lions, tigers, camels, goats and badgers are real; biffalo-buffalo-bisons, potamus, nosserus, bidgers and bodgers, wallaboo and mingo are muddled. And there is no bear with wings!
evidence: There are biffalo-buffalo-bisons, and a great big bear with wings,

questions.prompt: What does the child do at the zoo every time? Say the last line together.
facilitatorNotes: He gives buns to the elephant.
evidence: But I gave buns to the elephant when I went down to the Zoo!

questions.prompt: In the last stanza “gave” becomes “give” and “went” becomes “go.” What does that small change tell you?
facilitatorNotes: That he does it every time he goes: it is a habit he loves, not just one visit.
evidence: But I give buns to the elephant when I go down to the Zoo!

questions.prompt: Why does he like the elephant best, when there are lions and tigers?
facilitatorNotes: The other animals will not talk, shake hands or say “How do you do?”, but the elephant takes his buns. It is the animal he can make friends with.
evidence: You can’t shake hands with a mingo—he doesn’t like shaking hands.

readings.title: Missing
readings.challenge: Hear how the question about the mouse changes each time it is asked.
readings.focus: A child’s worry grows while a small pet is lost in a big house.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Christopher Robin lived in London, a very big city. A pet mouse lives in a box or cage. “Woffelly” is a made-up word; say it and wiggle your nose.

excerpt.locator: “Missing,” the whole poem; opens “Has anybody seen my mouse?”; closes “Hasn’t anybody seen my mouse?”.

questions.prompt: How did the mouse get out?
facilitatorNotes: The child opened the box for half a minute to check, and the mouse jumped out while he was looking.
evidence: And while I was looking, he jumped outside!

questions.prompt: Whom does the child ask? Listen to how the question changes, all the way to “Hasn’t anybody.”
facilitatorNotes: Anybody, Uncle John, Aunt Rose, and then everybody again. “Hasn’t anybody” sounds more worried, almost ready to cry.
evidence: Uncle John, have you seen my mouse?
Hasn’t anybody seen my mouse?

questions.prompt: Why does the child worry the mouse will be lonely and hungry?
facilitatorNotes: He is a country mouse, not a town one, so London will feel strange and there may be nothing for him to eat.
evidence: So he’ll feel all lonely in a London street;

questions.prompt: What is a “woffelly nose”? Why do you think the poet made up a word?
facilitatorNotes: A twitchy, sniffing nose. No ordinary word sounds quite right, so he makes one up, the way a child might.
evidence: Have you seen a mouse with a woffelly nose?

readings.title: Hoppity; At Home
readings.challenge: Hop along with the first poem, then listen for what the child wants in the second.
readings.focus: Two small poems about a child: one who cannot stop hopping, one who cannot wait for a toy.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A busby is a tall fur hat worn by some soldiers. The soldier wanted here is a toy soldier from a shop, and the shopman is the shopkeeper.

excerpt.locator: “Hoppity” and “At Home,” two whole poems; opens “Christopher Robin goes Hoppity, hoppity,”; closes “…to get one (He’s written to the shopman) Daddy’s going to get one as soon as he can come.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Christopher Robin say he cannot stop hopping?
facilitatorNotes: If he stopped hopping he could not go anywhere. It is a silly reason that makes perfect sense to him.
evidence: If he stopped hopping, he couldn’t go anywhere,

questions.prompt: Look at the end of “Hoppity”: the lines get shorter and shorter. How should we read them?
facilitatorNotes: Slower and slower, one hop for each line, until the last “Hop.” Try it standing up.
evidence: That’s why he always goes

questions.prompt: In “At Home,” what kind of soldier does the child want, and what would he give him?
facilitatorNotes: A tall red soldier in a busby who plays the drum; he would give him cream-cakes and cream for tea.
evidence: I want a soldier who plays on the drum.

questions.prompt: The words in brackets sound like little extra thoughts. Who might be saying them?
facilitatorNotes: The child, adding details as he imagines; or a grown-up explaining. Either is a fair reading.
evidence: (He’s written to the shopman)

readings.title: The Wrong House
readings.challenge: Listen for what each house is missing, one stanza after another.
readings.focus: A house can be big and grand and still not feel like a home if nobody loves what is in it.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A may-tree, or hawthorn, has white blossom in spring. A blackbird is a songbird. A hall here is a large entrance room.

excerpt.locator: “The Wrong House,” the whole poem; opens “I went into a house, and it wasn’t a house, It has big steps and a great big hall; But it…”; closes “…call. . . . But nobody listened to it, Nobody Liked it, Nobody wanted it at all.”.

questions.prompt: What is missing from the first house? The second? The third?
facilitatorNotes: A garden; a may-tree; a blackbird. Each house has more than the last, but still not enough.
evidence: But it hasn’t got a garden,
But it hasn’t got a may-tree,
But it hasn’t got a blackbird,

questions.prompt: In the last stanza the house has a may-tree and a blackbird. What is wrong now?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody listens to the blackbird, likes it or wants it. The trouble is now the people, not the house.
evidence: But nobody listened to it,

questions.prompt: What makes a house feel like a home, for the child in this poem?
facilitatorNotes: Growing things, a tree, birdsong, and people who listen and care about them. Children may add their own ideas.
evidence: It isn’t like a house at all.

readings.title: Summer Afternoon
readings.challenge: Count the cows, and then count again.
readings.focus: A quiet picture of a river, where the water shows a second picture.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. The brink is the edge of the water. A may-fly is a small insect that flutters over rivers. A swallow is a quick bird with a forked tail.

excerpt.locator: “Summer Afternoon,” the whole poem; opens “Six brown cows walk down to drink (All the little fishes blew bubbles at the may-fly).…”; closes “…from the water and six from the air; Up and down the river darts a blue-black swallow.”.

questions.prompt: How many cows walk down to drink? How many are there when they bend to drink? How can that be?
facilitatorNotes: Six walk down; twelve bend to drink, six real cows and six reflected in the water.
evidence: Six from the water and six from the air;

questions.prompt: What are the little fishes doing while the cows drink? What sounds can you hear?
facilitatorNotes: Blowing bubbles at the may-fly and waggling their tails; the cows splash and swish.
evidence: (All the little fishes went waggle-tail, waggle-tail)—

questions.prompt: The lines about the fishes are in brackets. Why might the poet put them there?
facilitatorNotes: They are a small quiet picture under the water, beside the big picture of the cows, like glancing down and back up. Accept other reasons.
evidence: (All the little fishes blew bubbles at the may-fly).

readings.title: The Dormouse and the Doctor
readings.challenge: Listen for the flowers’ colours each time they come back in brackets.
readings.focus: A busy doctor “cures” a happy dormouse of the one thing he loved, and the dormouse finds his own way back.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A dormouse is a small, sleepy mouse. Delphiniums are tall blue flowers and geraniums red ones; chrysanthemums are bushy flowers, here yellow and white. Doctors once asked patients to say “Ninety-nine” while they listened to the chest. Kent is a part of England famous for gardens; cuttings are pieces of plants for planting. Tonics were medicines meant to make you stronger.

excerpt.locator: “The Dormouse and the Doctor,” the whole poem; opens “There once was a Dormouse who lived in a bed Of delphiniums (blue) and geraniums (red),…”; closes “…(so Aunt Emily says) that he lies Fast asleep on his front with his paws to his eyes.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Dormouse love to look at? Say the line with the colours.
facilitatorNotes: Delphiniums (blue) and geraniums (red), which he can see all day from his bed.
evidence: Of delphiniums (blue) and geraniums (red).

questions.prompt: Is the Dormouse really ill? Why does the Doctor say he needs a change?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing in the poem says he is ill; he is simply in his flower bed. The Doctor just prefers chrysanthemums. Some children will say he must be ill because the Doctor came.
evidence: What the patient requires is a change,

questions.prompt: The Doctor keeps praising the chrysanthemums and himself. Who is he really thinking about?
facilitatorNotes: Himself and what he likes, not what the Dormouse likes.
evidence: These cases as I do! The cure has begun!

questions.prompt: How does the Dormouse make himself better in the end?
facilitatorNotes: He shuts his eyes with his paws and imagines his old blue and red flowers.
evidence: I’ll pretend the chrysanthemums turn to a bed

readings.title: Shoes and Stockings
readings.challenge: Listen for the two working sounds, and who makes each one.
readings.focus: Old workers in two hidden places make gold things for a bride, and the poem sounds like their work.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A cavern is a big cave. Dainty means small and delicate. A knight was a soldier of long ago who rode a horse. Old wives here means old women. To weave is to make cloth by crossing threads.

excerpt.locator: “Shoes and Stockings,” the whole poem; opens “There’s a cavern in the mountain where the old men meet (Hammer, hammer, hammer . . .…”; closes “…But she must have stockings on her dainty feet. Chatter, chatter, chatter . . . Chatter.”.

questions.prompt: Who makes the gold slippers, and where? Who makes the gold stockings?
facilitatorNotes: Old men in a cavern in the mountain make the slippers; old wives in a cottage by the river weave the stockings.
evidence: There’s a cavern in the mountain where the old men meet
There’s a cottage by the river where the old wives meet

questions.prompt: Why do the old men go “Hammer, hammer” and the old wives go “Chatter, chatter”?
facilitatorNotes: The men hammer metal into slippers; the women talk while they weave. The sounds tell us what each group is doing.
evidence: Hammer, hammer, hammer
Chatter, chatter, chatter

questions.prompt: Each stanza ends with one word alone. What does that sound like?
facilitatorNotes: The work slowing down and stopping, as if the job is done. Read the last word quietly.
evidence: Hammer.
Chatter.

questions.prompt: Whom are the slippers and stockings for, and why?
facilitatorNotes: For “my lady,” who is going to marry her true knight; she must look her best.
evidence: My lady is marrying her own true knight,

readings.title: Knights and Ladies
readings.challenge: Notice where the poem stops looking at a picture and starts looking up a hill.
readings.focus: A picture-book page and a row of trees make a child wonder whether long ago could still happen.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Knights rode horses long ago, in the Middle Ages, and squires were their helpers. Cobbles are rounded stones in an old street; eaves are the edges of a roof. A gage was a glove or token thrown down as a sign. Firs are tall evergreen trees.

excerpt.locator: “Knights and Ladies,” the whole poem; opens “There is in my old picture-book A page at which I like to look, Where knights and squires…”; closes “…as it would have been Those many, many years ago. . . . Perhaps I might. You never know.”.

questions.prompt: What does the child see on the page of the old picture-book?
facilitatorNotes: Knights and squires riding down a steep cobbled street, and ladies waving handkerchiefs and tossing down gages.
evidence: Where knights and squires come riding down

questions.prompt: What does the child see in real life that makes him think of knights?
facilitatorNotes: The fir trees coming down the hill two by two, like riders in a line.
evidence: The firs come marching, two by two,

questions.prompt: The poem ends, “Perhaps I might. You never know.” Does the child really believe a knight might come?
facilitatorNotes: Half believing and half playing. Some children will say yes, some no; either can be supported.
evidence: Perhaps I might. You never know.

readings.title: Little Bo-Peep and Little Boy-Blue
readings.challenge: Take turns: one reader is Bo-Peep and one is Boy Blue. Listen for who is asking.
readings.focus: Two nursery-rhyme shepherds who both lost their sheep talk their way to a promise.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Bo-Peep and Boy Blue come from old nursery rhymes: Bo-Peep lost her sheep, and Boy Blue fell asleep instead of blowing his horn to call them. Here they talk to each other. Each stanza is a question and an answer, so read it in two voices.

excerpt.locator: “Little Bo-Peep and Little Boy-Blue,” the whole poem; opens ““What have you done with your sheep, Little Bo-Peep? What have you done with your sheep,…”; closes “…Boy Blue, my dear, Keep near, keep very near.” “I shall be always here, Little Bo-Peep.””.

questions.prompt: How did each of them lose their sheep?
facilitatorNotes: Bo-Peep lost every one, and seems to think it fun; Boy Blue’s sheep went off while he was asleep.
evidence: I’ve lost them, every one!
Went off, when I was asleep.

questions.prompt: How does each one plan to get the sheep back? What does the other think of the plan?
facilitatorNotes: Bo-Peep will wait for them to come home to tea; Boy Blue will blow his horn for an hour. Each gently teases the other’s plan.
evidence: They’ll all come home to tea.
Isn’t that rather slow,

questions.prompt: How does the talk change in the last stanzas?
facilitatorNotes: From sheep to getting married and where they will live, up in the hills with the sheep.
evidence: I’d like to marry you.

questions.prompt: At the end Bo-Peep says, “Keep near, keep very near.” Why might she ask that?
facilitatorNotes: Perhaps because so much in their lives wanders off, sheep included, and she wants this to stay. Boy Blue promises he always will. Accept other readings.
evidence: Keep near, keep very near.
I shall be always here,

readings.title: The Invaders
readings.challenge: Picture the wood before, while and after the cows walk through it.
readings.focus: A spring wood holds its breath while the cows pass, and then bursts into song.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Primroses are pale yellow spring flowers, anemones are white, violets small and purple, and bluebells blue. A ride is a wide path through a wood. A yew is a dark evergreen tree, and an outpost is a lookout place. An anthem is a song of praise. Invaders are those who come into a place that is not theirs.

excerpt.locator: “The Invaders,” the whole poem; opens “In careless patches through the wood The clumps of yellow primrose stood, And sheets of…”; closes “…line had passed. . . . Then all the wood began to sing Its morning anthem to the spring.”.

questions.prompt: What flowers grow in the wood? What colour is each one?
facilitatorNotes: Yellow primroses, white anemones like snow, hidden violets, and bluebells bluer than ever.
evidence: The clumps of yellow primrose stood,

questions.prompt: How do the cows walk through the wood?
facilitatorNotes: Slowly, one by one, in silence, breathing the morning air and leaving it sweeter.
evidence: The cows came slowly, one by one,

questions.prompt: Why might the poet call the cows “invaders”? What does the wood do while they pass?
facilitatorNotes: They come marching through the birds’ and flowers’ wood like a line of soldiers, and the whole wood goes still, waiting. Some children will say the cows are gentle, not really invaders; that is worth talking about.
evidence: But all the little wood was still,

questions.prompt: What happens when the blackbird whistles? Why does everyone wait for him?
facilitatorNotes: He is like a lookout: when he whistles that the line has passed, the whole wood starts its morning song to spring.
evidence: Then all the wood began to sing

readings.title: Before Tea
readings.challenge: Listen for all the lines that end with the sound “-een.”
readings.focus: A girl who was told her hands were dirty disappears, and comes back with a very grand answer.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A green here is a grassy space in a village or park. “Purfickly” is how a small child might say “perfectly.” The Queen was the queen of England.

excerpt.locator: “Before Tea,” the whole poem; opens “Emmeline Has not been seen For more than a week. She slipped between The two tall trees…”; closes “…Said, “Sillies, I went and saw the Queen. She says my hands are purfickly clean!””.

questions.prompt: Where did Emmeline go, and what did the other children do?
facilitatorNotes: She slipped between the two tall trees at the end of the green; they went after her, calling her name.
evidence: The two tall trees at the end of the green . . .

questions.prompt: Someone says, “I didn’t mean—.” What do you think happened before Emmeline left?
facilitatorNotes: Someone told her her hands were not clean, and she was hurt or cross and went off.
evidence: I only said that your hands weren’t clean.

questions.prompt: Where does Emmeline say she has been? Do you believe her?
facilitatorNotes: To see the Queen, who said her hands are perfectly clean: the best answer to whoever complained. Some children will believe her; others think she is pretending. Both are fair.
evidence: Sillies, I went and saw the Queen.

questions.prompt: The poem is called “Before Tea,” but the children say she was gone more than a week. How can both be true?
facilitatorNotes: To worried children a short time felt like a week; or they are exaggerating. The title hints she was back before tea.
evidence: For more than a week.

readings.title: Bad Sir Brian Botany
readings.challenge: Listen to how the chorus “I am Sir Brian!” changes, and who is saying it each time.
readings.focus: A bully knight gets a taste of his own medicine and becomes plain Mr. Botany.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. A battleaxe is a big axe for fighting, and spurs are spiky points on a rider’s boots. “Blipped” is a made-up word for bonked. Ironical salutes are pretend bows that really make fun of someone. Duckweed is a green plant floating on ponds, and breeches are trousers. A title is a name like “Sir”; Esquire is a polite word added after a plain man’s name.
readings.contentNote: Sir Brian hits villagers on the head and kicks them into the pond; later the villagers bonk him, throw him in ditches and push him under waterfalls. It is all told as slapstick.

excerpt.locator: “Bad Sir Brian Botany,” the whole poem; opens “Sir Brian had a battleaxe with great big knobs on; He went among the villagers and…”; closes “…no! I am Sir Brian? Who’s he? I haven’t got any title, I’m Botany— Plain Mr. Botany (B).””.

questions.prompt: What does Sir Brian do to the villagers? On which days?
facilitatorNotes: Blips them on the head with his battleaxe on Wednesdays and Saturdays, and kicks them into the pond on Tuesdays and Fridays.
evidence: He went among the villagers and blipped them on the head.
He’d collect the passing villagers and kick them in the pond.

questions.prompt: What changes the morning he can’t find his battleaxe?
facilitatorNotes: Without it the villagers are not afraid. They crowd round him, make fun of him, and then do to him what he did to them.
evidence: And the villagers were round him with ironical salutes.

questions.prompt: Listen to the chorus: first “I am Sir Brian!”, then “You are Sir Brian?”, then “I am Sir Brian? Oh, no!” What does the change show?
facilitatorNotes: First he boasts; then the villagers mock him; at last he no longer wants to be Sir Brian at all. The same words tell how he has changed.
evidence: “You are Sir Brian? Indeed!
“I am Sir Brian? Oh, no!

questions.prompt: Was it right for the villagers to treat Sir Brian the way he treated them?
facilitatorNotes: He learned his lesson and changed; but they became bullies too for a day. Many children will cheer; others will say two wrongs don’t make a right. Both deserve a hearing.
evidence: They pulled him out and dried him, and they blipped him on the head.
He is quite a different person now he hasn’t got his spurs on,

readings.title: In the Fashion
readings.challenge: Listen to what the child has to say to the animals at the beginning and at the end.
readings.focus: A child who feels left out imagines buying a tail, to be just like everyone else.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Something “in the fashion” is what everyone is wearing or doing right now. Sixpence was a small English coin. A quail is a small, round bird.

excerpt.locator: “In the Fashion,” the whole poem; opens “A lion has a tail and a very fine tail, And so has an elephant, and so has a whale, And…”; closes “…whale! And, look! There’s a crocodile! He’s got a tail! “You’ve all got tails like me!””.

questions.prompt: Which animals have tails? Who doesn’t?
facilitatorNotes: A lion, an elephant, a whale, a crocodile and a quail; the child has none.
evidence: They’ve all got tails but me.

questions.prompt: How would the child get a tail? What would happen then?
facilitatorNotes: Buy one with sixpence at a shop and try it on; then all the animals would come round to see.
evidence: If I had sixpence I would buy one;

questions.prompt: At the end the child says, “You’ve all got tails like me!” Why turn it round that way?
facilitatorNotes: Now the child is not the odd one out but the one everyone matches. It is a funny way to show how much the child wants to belong. Some children will just enjoy the joke; that is a good reading too.
evidence: You’ve all got tails like me!

readings.title: If I Were King; Vespers
readings.challenge: In the first poem, listen for what the child would do as king; in the second, for what Christopher Robin thinks about while he prays.
readings.focus: Two small poems about a child’s mind: wishing to be king, and wandering off during prayers.
readings.context: From A. A. Milne’s When We Were Very Young (1924), poems written for and about his small son, Christopher Robin. Norroway is an old name for Norway; Babylon was a great city long ago, and Timbuctoo a far-off city in Africa. A mantelpiece is a shelf above a fireplace. Vespers are evening prayers. A dressing-gown is a robe, and Nanny is the woman who looks after the child.

excerpt.locator: “If I Were King” and “Vespers,” two whole poems; opens “I often wish I were a King, And then I could do anything.”; closes “…little gold head. Hush! Hush! Whisper who dares! Christopher Robin is saying his prayers.”.

questions.prompt: What would the child do as King of Spain, France or Greece? Are these big kingly things?
facilitatorNotes: Take off his hat in the rain, not brush his hair for aunts, push things off the mantelpiece. They are small things grown-ups do not allow, which is the joke.
evidence: I wouldn’t brush my hair for aunts.
I’d push things off the mantelpiece.

questions.prompt: In “Vespers,” what does Christopher Robin think about while he is praying?
facilitatorNotes: His bath, Nanny’s blue dressing-gown, his own dressing-gown with a hood and hiding in it, and trying to remember what else to say.
evidence: Wasn’t it fun in the bath to-night?
If I open my fingers a little bit more,

questions.prompt: What is the last thing he remembers to pray? Why might it have taken him so long?
facilitatorNotes: “God bless Me.” Children may say he was busy thinking about other things, or that it is funny he forgot himself last.
evidence: Oh! Now I remember it. God bless Me.

questions.prompt: The first and last stanzas of “Vespers” say “Hush! Hush! Whisper who dares!” Who is speaking those lines, and why do they whisper?
facilitatorNotes: A grown-up watching, not wanting to disturb him. Inside, the poem lets us hear his wandering thoughts, while the grown-up sees only a quiet, praying child. Some children will say it is the poet, or us; any watcher who loves him fits.
evidence: Hush! Hush! Whisper who dares!
